title: Looking back: a free hand with Raeburn
summary: Handy says it was an exciting time with a free hand to write and he would let himself write again.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: else left that we want to say about the Boyd Raeburn days?
Boyd Raeburn days were-high point is not the right word--
It was a very exciting time of life.
It was exciting, but it's also the place where you had the most leverage; do I express that well?
Leverage in what? What do you mean?
In what you wanted to do. You were able to lay down your own--
Right, I had a free hand, as far as the writing was concerned. I wasn't directed or told what to do or how to write. That's true.
If you had another shot at those days, would you do anything different?
No. I would let myself write.
Yes.
Back on the air.
Was that a clear interview, I wouldn't have said that otherwise?
Knowing what I know now?
Knowing what you know now, would you have liked to have done it differently? That's an open end cliche, we call it, in the interview business.

It's hard to say what I would do now. I would be a little wiser on how to write, I would be writing bettter today, considering the years of experience I've had since then. I feel the same way inside of me about letting it come out.
What would have happened if you had been able to lay this gift in front of Stan or Woody or Gene Krupa or Bobby Sherwood?
I don't know.
It's only happened that you were with Boyd at the moment; would the same thing have happened, you suppose?
Probably there would have been much more back and forth with these other people, since they were more musicians than Boyd was.

I think Boyd was stunned at first; he didn't know what the hell was happening. He just knew enough to be quiet and let it happen. As time went on he got to be able to relax a little until it got to a point where he started telling people he was responsible for it.
